h: Deer park, nature reserve and a famous film beach
p: Holkham was built between the 1730s and 1760s for Thomas Coke, 1st Earl of Leicester, who came back from his Grand Tour of Europe with a head full of classical ideas and a load of art to show off. William Kent had a big hand in the design, and that's why the whole place feels like a slice of ancient Rome dropped into Norfolk. A later Coke, known as Coke of Norfolk, became famous as a farming pioneer, so the estate has a strong place in the history of British agriculture too.

Out in the park, look out for the herd of fallow deer, which you'll often spot grazing under the trees. The lake is lovely for a gentle walk, and the obelisk and monuments give you something to aim for as you go.

Then there's the beach. Holkham's sweep of sand is part of the Holkham National Nature Reserve, and it's appeared on the big screen, most famously in the closing scene of Shakespeare in Love. Lady Anne's Drive takes you from the main road to the pinewoods and dunes, and it's a cracking spot for birdwatching in winter when huge flocks of geese fly in.
Give it a full day if you want house, park and beach. Pack a picnic, a windproof and a spare pair of socks.

Nearby, the Victoria Inn at Holkham is handy for a meal, Burnham Market has posh little shops, and Burnham Thorpe is where Admiral Nelson was born. From Wells you can also hop on the narrow-gauge Wells and Walsingham Light Railway.
